articles.title: ID2Pattern: How Payment Risk Models Pretrain on High-Cardinality Identity Fields Without Exploding Vocabulary
articles.excerpt: Payment risk agents face a vocabulary explosion problem. Every new card, device fingerprint, or account ID expands the embedding table. Traditional categorical encoding approaches either maintain a gr…
articles.body: Payment risk agents face a vocabulary explosion problem. Every new card, device fingerprint, or account ID expands the embedding table. Traditional categorical encoding approaches either maintain a growing lookup table or hash identities into fixed buckets, losing behavioral signal in the process. ID2Pattern, a pretraining framework from a recent ArXiv paper (2610.41988v1), encodes identity behavior patterns instead of identity values. The model learns how identities behave across transaction sequences without memorizing specific card numbers or device IDs. When a new card appears at inference time, the model generalizes from learned patterns rather than failing on an out-of-vocabulary token.

articles.title: The Newspaper of One: Inside a Lights-Out Publishing System
articles.excerpt: The Newspaper of One: Inside a Lights-Out Publishing System For most of publishing history, the bottleneck was production. Type had to be set, pages had to be laid out, presses had to roll, and every…
articles.body: The Newspaper of One: Inside a Lights-Out Publishing System For most of publishing history, the bottleneck was production. Type had to be set, pages had to be laid out, presses had to roll, and every word of copy had to pass through a chain of human hands. The economics of media were really the economics of coordination: how many editors, typesetters, and distribution workers could you afford? That constraint is gone. What replaced it is stranger than most commentary admits. The scarce resource in publishing today is not production capacity, and it is not even attention exactly.

articles.title: Why "sent" isn't "delivered": tracking transactional email in Node.js with webhooks
articles.excerpt: A user clicks "Forgot password", your API returns 200, and ten minutes later they open a support ticket: the email never came. You check your logs and find email sent successfully. So what happened? U…
articles.body: A user clicks "Forgot password", your API returns 200, and ten minutes later they open a support ticket: the email never came. You check your logs and find email sent successfully . So what happened? Usually the answer is that "sent" only ever meant "some server accepted my request". Getting that email to the user is a separate step, and if your app doesn't track it, you're guessing. This post walks through modelling the lifecycle of a transactional email properly in Node.js: what each status means, how to send safely with retries, and how to consume delivery webhooks without getting duplicate or forged events.

articles.title: Rebuilding the Salesforce trigger framework as a baseline
articles.excerpt: Every Salesforce project I have worked on eventually grows a trigger framework. It starts as a single trigger with an if statement, becomes an interface with a dispatcher, and ends with a static Set t…
articles.body: Every Salesforce project I have worked on eventually grows a trigger framework. It starts as a single trigger with an if statement, becomes an interface with a dispatcher, and ends with a static Set<Id> that someone is afraid to touch. The code is rarely the problem. The problem is the contract: when a handler runs, when it does not, what happens on re-entry, and who is allowed to bypass it. This article walks through the baseline I built to stop rebuilding that contract on every project. It is deliberately small: 21 production Apex classes, 10 test classes, one trigger, custom metadata for configuration, and a permission set. The interesting parts are the decisions, not the class count.

articles.body: The Legacy Migration Dilemma Transitioning an aging on-premise legacy system—often built on monolithic architectures, outdated SQL servers, or messy file-based stores—to a modern cloud-native stack is one of the highest-stakes projects an enterprise can undertake. Business continuity depends on absolute data integrity. A single dropped foreign key or out-of-sync timestamp during a cutover can corrupt historical ledgers, halt fulfillment, or breach compliance. Operating out of Kochi, I frequently consult with traditional businesses and growing enterprises looking to overhaul brittle systems.

articles.body: TL;DR A top Android tinkerer has confirmed that you’ll lose app casting capabilities if you root your Googlebook. This is apparently because your Googlebook will no longer pass hardware key attestation. Googlebooks have been on the market for roughly a month now, and they have a few selling points. Unfortunately, it looks like you’ll lose out on one key feature if you choose to root your Googlebook. The developer explained that this is because the phone rejects app casting if the Googlebook doesn’t pass hardware key attestation.

articles.body: TL;DR Several Lenovo Smart Clock units are showing the incorrect time in many parts of Canada. Canada recently adopted daylight saving time permanently, but Lenovo Smart Clocks haven’t updated correctly. The issue reportedly occurs on both the Clock and Clock Essential models. Several territories in Canada recently flipped the decades-long tradition of changing clocks at the start and end of winter, permanently switching to permanent daylight saving time. That includes Alberta, parts of British Columbia, Manitoba, Northwestern Ontario, Saskatchewan, and Yukon. While that saves you the mental exercise of adjusting time every time at the major change of the seasons, big tech companies, including Lenovo, may have been scrambling to implement the change smoothly.

articles.title: Planetary defense: How military and civil satellites are watching fireballs to help keep Earth safe from space rocks
articles.excerpt: Satellites are watching fireballs blaze through Earth's atmosphere, strengthening planetary defense knowhow and helping scientists learn more about space debris impacts.
articles.body: It came from outer space, exploding high above the South Atlantic off the coast of Argentina. That April 1 event — an incoming meteor , also termed a bolide — was observed by both U.S. space-based military and civil sensors. Hush-hush U.S. government satellite sensors detected the speedy fireball cutting through our atmosphere. The object's brightness peaked at an altitude of nearly 60 miles (90.5 kilometers) over the South Atlantic. That dazzling spectacle was also caught by the National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration's GOES-E and Europe's Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Imager-1 satellite. Those two independent spacecraft in geostationary orbit detected the bolide via onboard lightning imagers.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 1, 1962: The Soviet Union Launches Mars 1 spacecraft to Red Planet during the Space Race
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. While it did end up flying by Mars , the mission was not exactly a success. After it separated from the rocket, it deployed its solar panels and started cruising toward Mars. When mission controllers were checking out the telemetry it transmitted back to Earth, they found out that Mars 1 had sprung a leak in one of the gas valves that controls the spacecraft's orientation. And without a working orientation system, Mars 1 would have a hard time pointing its antennas in the right direction. It lost contact with Earth when it was about halfway to Mars . A model of Mars 1, a Mars flyby spacecraft launched to the Red Planet by the Soviet Union on Nov. 1, 1962.

articles.excerpt: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
articles.body: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont.
